This is the homework 3!

#Problem 1
Load the NOAA data
```{r}
library(patchwork)
library(ggridges)
library(tidyverse)
library(p8105.datasets)
```

Check the number of rows and columns.
Check first 5 row of dataset to look variables.
```{r}
data("ny_noaa")
nrow(ny_noaa)
ncol(ny_noaa)
head(ny_noaa)
```
Check missing values in each variable
```{r}
colSums(is.na(ny_noaa))
```
The ny_noaa dataset contains 2,595,176 observations and 7 variables.

The dataset includes station ID (id), date (date), precipitation (prcp), snowfall (snow), snow depth (snwd), maximum temperature (tmax), and minimum temperature (tmin).Each row represents a weather observation for a station on a specific date.

There are no missing values in id or date.
Missing data are present in the weather variables, with 145,838 missing values in prcp, 381,221 in snow, 591,786 in snwd, 1,134,358 in tmax, and 1,134,420 in tmin.

Missing data are big issue in this dataset, especially for the temperature.


Separate date into year, month, and day.
Then check.
```{r}
ny_noaa =
  ny_noaa |>
  separate(date, into = c("year", "month", "day"), sep = "-")
```

Ensure observations for temperature, precipitation, and snowfall are given in reasonable units.
Convert temperature to Celsius.
```{r}
ny_noaa =
  ny_noaa |>
  mutate(
    tmax = as.numeric(tmax) / 10,
    tmin = as.numeric(tmin) / 10
  )
```

For snowfall, what are the most commonly observed values? Why?
```{r}
ny_noaa =
  ny_noaa |>
  mutate(prcp = prcp / 10)
```
According to the data description, precipitation, maximum temperature, and minimum temperature were originally measured in tenths of their respective units.
I divided prcp, tmax, and tmin by 10 so that precipitation is measured in millimeters and temperature is measured in degrees Celsius.
snow and snwd were already measured in millimeters.


```{r}
ny_noaa |>
  count(snow) |>
  arrange(desc(n))
```
The most commonly observed snowfall value is 0 mm, with 2,008,508 observations.
I think because most days do not have snowfall.

Make a two-panel plot showing the average max temperature in January and in July in each station across years. Is there any observable / interpretable structure? Any outliers?

Keep January and July observations
```{r}
ny_noaa_jan_july =
  ny_noaa |>
  filter(month == "01" | month == "07")
```

Calculate average maximum temperature
In my first attempt, I got NaN values when calculating the mean because some stations had missing tmax values. So I used drop_na(tmax) before calculating the average maximum temperature.
```{r}
jan_july_tmax =
  ny_noaa_jan_july |>
  drop_na(tmax) |>
  group_by(id, year, month) |>
  summarize(mean_tmax = mean(tmax))
```
Change year to numeric
```{r}
jan_july_tmax =
  jan_july_tmax |>
  mutate(year = as.numeric(year))
```

Plot average maximum temperature in January and July

```{r}
jan_july_tmax |>
  ggplot(aes(x = year, y = mean_tmax)) +
  geom_point(alpha = .5) +
  facet_grid(. ~ month) +
  labs(
    title = "Average Maximum Temperature in January and July",
    x = "Year",
    y = "Average Maximum Temperature (C)"
  ) +
  scale_x_continuous(
    breaks = c(1981, 1990, 2000, 2010)
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
```

Average maximum temperatures are much lower in January than in July.
Average temperatures in January range from -10°C to 10°C, while average temperatures in July range from 20°C to 30°C.
There are some outliers.A January value around -13°C and a July value around 14°C.


Make a two-panel plot showing (i) tmax vs tmin for the full dataset (note that a scatterplot may not be the best option); 

Remove missing temperature values
```{r}
tmax_tmin =
  ny_noaa |>
  drop_na(tmax, tmin)
```

Plot maximum and minimum temperature
```{r}
tmax_tmin_plot =
  tmax_tmin |>
  ggplot(aes(x = tmin, y = tmax)) +
  geom_hex() +
  labs(
    title = "Maximum vs Minimum Temperature",
    x = "Minimum Temperature (C)",
    y = "Maximum Temperature (C)"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
```
and (ii) make a plot showing the distribution of snowfall values greater than 0 and less than 100 separately by year.

Keep snowfall values between 0 and 100 mm
Change year to a factor
```{r}
snowfall_df =
  ny_noaa |>
  filter(snow > 0, snow < 100) |>
  mutate(year = factor(year))
```

Plot snowfall distribution by year
```{r}
snowfall_plot =
  snowfall_df |>
  ggplot(aes(x = snow, y = year)) +
  geom_density_ridges(scale = .85) +
  labs(
    title = "Snowfall Distribution by Year",
    x = "Snowfall (mm)",
    y = "Year"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
```

Combine the two plots
```{r}
snowfall_plot + tmax_tmin_plot
```

#Problem 2

Read demographic data and accelerometer data and check

I checked the first five rows of the demographic data and found that the first four rows contain variable descriptions and coding information. Therefore, I skipped the first four rows.
```{r}
demographic_df = read_csv("./data/nhanes_covar.csv", skip = 4)
accelerometer_df = read_csv("./data/nhanes_accel.csv")
head(demographic_df)
head(accelerometer_df)
```


Load, tidy, merge, and otherwise organize the data sets. Your final dataset should include all originally observed variables；

exclude participants less than 21 years of age, and those with missing demographic data
```{r}
demographic_df =
  demographic_df |>
  filter(age >= 21) |>
  drop_na()
```

Tidy accelerometer data
```{r}
accelerometer_df =
  accelerometer_df |>
  pivot_longer(
    min1:min1440,
    names_to = "minute",
    values_to = "MIMS"
  )
```

After knitting the document, I found that the 24-hour activity plot did not display the time correctly because the minute variable was stored as character values. Therefore, I further cleaned the minute variable before the analysis.
```{r}
accelerometer_df =
  accelerometer_df |>
  separate(
    minute,
    into = c("min", "minute"),
    sep = 3
  )
accelerometer_df =
  accelerometer_df |>
  mutate(minute = as.numeric(minute)) |>
  select(-min)
head(accelerometer_df)
```

Merge demographic and accelerometer data
```{r}
merged_df =
  left_join(demographic_df, accelerometer_df, by = "SEQN")
```

Change sex to a factor
```{r}
merged_df =
  merged_df |>
  mutate(
    sex = factor(
      sex,
      levels = c(1, 2),
      labels = c("Male", "Female")
    )
  )
```

Change education to an ordered factor
```{r}
merged_df =
  merged_df |>
  mutate(
    education = factor(
      education,
      levels = c(1, 2, 3),
      labels = c(
        "Less than high school",
        "High school equivalent",
        "More than high school"
      ),
      ordered = TRUE
    )
  )
```

Produce a reader-friendly table for the number of men and women in each education category

Keep one row for each participant
```{r}
participant_df =
  merged_df |>
  distinct(SEQN, sex, age, BMI, education)
```

Count participants by education and sex
```{r}
participant_table =
  participant_df |>
  count(education, sex) |>
  pivot_wider(
    names_from = sex,
    values_from = n
  )
participant_table
```

create a visualization of the age distributions for men and women in each education category

Plot age distributions by sex and education
```{r}
participant_df |>
  ggplot(aes(x = sex, y = age, color = sex)) +
  geom_boxplot() +
  facet_grid(. ~ education) +
  labs(
    title = "Age Distribution by Sex and Education",
    x = "Sex",
    y = "Age",
    color = "Sex"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
```

In the "less than high school" and "more than high school" groups, the number of males and females is about the same. 
In the "high school equivalent" group, there are more males than females. 

The age distribution shows that participants with less than high school education are generally older, while participants with more than high school education are generally younger. 

In the "high school equivalent" group, females are generally older than males.


Calculate total activity for each participant
```{r}
total_activity_df =
  merged_df |>
  group_by(SEQN, sex, age, education) |>
  summarize(total_activity = sum(MIMS))
```
Plot these total activities (y-axis) against age (x-axis); your plot should compare men to women and have separate panels for each education level. Include a trend line or a smooth.

Plot total activity against age
```{r}
total_activity_df |>
  ggplot(aes(x = age, y = total_activity, color = sex)) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_smooth(se = FALSE) +
  facet_grid(. ~ education) +
  labs(
    title = "Total Activity by Age, Sex, and Education",
    x = "Age",
    y = "Total Activity",
    color = "Sex"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
```

In all three education groups, total activity decreases as people get older. There are some differences between males and females, but the pattern is different in each group. Overall, older participants have lower total activity than younger participants.


Make a three-panel plot that shows the 24-hour activity time courses for each education level and use color to indicate sex. 

Calculate average activity for each minute
```{r}
activity_time_df =
  merged_df |>
  group_by(education, sex, minute) |>
  summarize(mean_MIMS = mean(MIMS)) |>
  ungroup()
```
Plot 24-hour activity time courses
```{r}
activity_time_df |>
  ggplot(aes(x = minute, y = mean_MIMS, color = sex)) +
  geom_line() +
  facet_grid(. ~ education) +
  scale_x_continuous(
    breaks = c(0, 360, 720, 1080, 1440),
    labels = c("0", "6", "12", "18", "24")
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "24-Hour Activity by Sex and Education",
    x = "Hour",
    y = "Mean MIMS",
    color = "Sex"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
```

Activity is low at night. It goes up quickly in the morning, stays high during the day, and goes down in the evening. 
The daily pattern is similar in all three education groups. There are some differences between males and females.
In the "more than high school" group, females usually have more activity during the day.


#Problem 3
Read Citi Bike data
```{r}
jan_2020_df = read_csv("./data/Jan 2020 Citi.csv")
july_2020_df = read_csv("./data/July 2020 Citi.csv")
jan_2024_df = read_csv("./data/Jan 2024 Citi.csv")
july_2024_df = read_csv("./data/July 2024 Citi.csv")
```
Check Citi Bike data
```{r}
head(jan_2020_df)
head(july_2020_df)
head(jan_2024_df)
head(july_2024_df)
```

Add year and month
```{r}
jan_2020_df =
  jan_2020_df |>
  mutate(
    year = 2020,
    month = "January"
  )

july_2020_df =
  july_2020_df |>
  mutate(
    year = 2020,
    month = "July"
  )

jan_2024_df =
  jan_2024_df |>
  mutate(
    year = 2024,
    month = "January"
  )

july_2024_df =
  july_2024_df |>
  mutate(
    year = 2024,
    month = "July"
  )
```

Combine Citi Bike data
```{r}
citi_df =
  bind_rows(
    jan_2020_df,
    july_2020_df,
    jan_2024_df,
    july_2024_df
  )
head(citi_df)
```

Check year and month
```{r}
citi_df |>
  count(year, month)
```
Check the size of the combined data
```{r}
nrow(citi_df)
ncol(citi_df)
```
The combined Citi Bike dataset has 99,485 rides and 9 variables. 
The data comes from January and July in both 2020 and 2024. 
These variables are ride ID, bike type, weekday, ride duration, start and end station names, membership type, year, and month.


Produce a reader-friendly table showing the total number of rides in each combination of year and month separating casual riders and Citi Bike members. Comment on these results.

Create a reader-friendly table
```{r}
ride_count_df =
  citi_df |>
  count(year, month, member_casual)

ride_count_table =
  ride_count_df |>
  pivot_wider(
    names_from = member_casual,
    values_from = n
  )
ride_count_table
```

There are more member rides than casual rides in all four groups. 
January 2020 has much fewer casual rides than the other groups, while July 2024 has much more member rides.

Make a table showing the 5 most popular starting stations for July 2024; include the number of rides originating from these stations.

Keep rides from July 2024
```{r}
july_2024 =
  citi_df |>
  filter(year == 2024, month == "July")
```

Count 5 most popular starting station
```{r}
july_2024 |>
  count(start_station_name) |>
  arrange(desc(n)) |>
  head(5)
```

These are the top five starting stations in July 2024.

Make a plot to investigate the effects of day of the week, month, and year on median ride duration. This plot can include one or more panels, but should facilitate comparison across all variables of interest. Comment on your observations from this plot.

Calculate median ride duration
```{r}
median_duration_df =
  citi_df |>
  group_by(year, month, weekdays) |>
  summarize(median_duration = median(duration)) |>
  ungroup()
```
Order weekdays
I changed the weekday labels to shorter names to make the x-axis easier to read.
```{r}
median_duration_df =
  median_duration_df |>
  mutate(
    weekdays = factor(
      weekdays,
      levels = c(
        "Monday", "Tuesday", "Wednesday", "Thursday",
        "Friday", "Saturday", "Sunday"
      ),
      labels = c(
        "Mon", "Tue", "Wed", "Thu",
        "Fri", "Sat", "Sun"
      ),
      ordered = TRUE
    )
  )
```

```{r}
median_duration_df |>
  ggplot(aes(x = weekdays, y = median_duration, color = month, group = month)) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_line() +
  facet_grid(. ~ year) +
  labs(
    title = "Median Ride Duration by Weekday, Month, and Year",
    x = "Weekday",
    y = "Median Ride Duration (minutes)",
    color = "Month"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
```

Median ride duration is higher in July than in January for both years. Ride duration is also generally higher in 2020 than in 2024. Weekend rides, especially on Saturday and Sunday, tend to have longer median durations than weekday rides.

There were relatively few electric Citi Bikes in 2020, but many more are available now. For data in 2024, make a figure that shows the impact of month, membership status, and bike type on the distribution of ride duration. Comment on your results.

Keep rides from 2024 and check bike types
```{r}
citi_2024 =
  citi_df |>
  filter(year == 2024)
citi_2024 |>
  count(rideable_type)
```

Plot ride duration distributions in 2024
```{r}
citi_2024 |>
  ggplot(aes(x = duration, color = rideable_type)) +
  geom_density() +
  facet_grid(member_casual ~ month) +
  labs(
    title = "Ride Duration Distribution in 2024",
    x = "Ride Duration (minutes)",
    y = "Density",
    color = "Bike Type"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
```

In all groups, ride duration is right-skewed. This means most rides are short. 
Casual riders have a wider range of ride times than members, mostly in July. 
The patterns for classic bikes and electric bikes are about the same.
